content: The survey included individuals who were at least 18 years old and living with hepatitis B. A total of 550 eligible participants from 76 countries completed the survey. National hepatitis program managers from 30 countries were surveyed to gather their perspectives on new directions in hepatitis B care, treatment, and prevention of mother-to-child transmission of hepatitis B virus (HBV PMTCT). A global online survey was conducted among healthcare workers to better understand the challenges of delivering hepatitis B care in resource-limited settings. This 53-item survey addressed the accessibility of diagnostic tests and therapies, as well as priorities for achieving the goal of hepatitis B elimination. An online survey was also conducted among nine networks of pediatricians who provide care to children and adolescents with hepatitis B. These networks included PENTA Child Health Network, FISPGHAN (Federation of International Societies of Pediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology, and Nutrition), APPSPGHAN (Asia Pacific), CAPGAN (Commonwealth), ESPGHAN (Europe), LASPGHAN (Latin America), NASPGHAN (North America), and PASPGHAN (Pan Arab). The quality of evidence and the strength of recommendations were assessed using the GRADE methodology, which was adapted for diagnostic tests and strategies. The GRADE system separates the certainty of evidence from the strength of recommendations. Certainty of evidence reflects confidence that the reported estimates of effect are sufficient to support a specific recommendation. Evidence is classified as high, moderate, low, or very low certainty. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are initially rated as high-quality evidence but may be downgraded due to factors such as risk of bias, inconsistency of results, indirectness of evidence, imprecision, or publication bias. Observational studies are initially rated as low-quality evidence but may be upgraded if the treatment effect is very large, if there is evidence of a dose-response relationship, or if all plausible biases would underestimate the effect. The strength of a recommendation reflects the extent to which the desirable effects of following the recommendation outweigh the potential undesirable effects. Recommendations are classified as either strong or conditional. A strong recommendation is based on high-quality evidence and indicates that the benefits clearly outweigh the harms. Conditional recommendations are made when the desirable effects probably outweigh the undesirable effects, but the trade-offs are less certain or the benefits are relatively small compared to the harms. The GRADE system considers several factors when determining the strength of recommendations, including the balance of benefits and harms, the certainty of evidence, values and preferences of stakeholders, cost and financial implications, feasibility, and equity. Strong recommendations are more likely when the intervention is cost-effective, widely acceptable, feasible, and has a positive impact on equity. The Guidelines Development Group (GDG) reviewed systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and complementary information to ensure understanding and agreement on scoring criteria. The GRADE method was used to rate the certainty of evidence and determine the strength of recommendations. Recommendations were formulated based on the balance of benefits and harms, the quality of evidence, and other factors. Consensus was reached for all recommendations without the need for voting. Conflicts of interest were managed according to WHO policies. All external contributors completed declarations of interest forms. The WHO Steering Group reviewed these declarations to assess potential conflicts. Participants with significant conflicts of interest were allowed to contribute technical expertise but were excluded from voting on specific topics. No individual was excluded from the GDG entirely. The guidelines and recommendations will be disseminated electronically via the WHO website, regional offices, and country offices, as well as through webinars, conferences, and peer-reviewed publications. Implementation will be supported by integration into national treatment programs and monitoring frameworks. Updates to the guidelines will be based on new evidence and user needs. Expanded treatment eligibility and key topics addressed in the guidelines include non-invasive assessment of liver disease stage, criteria for determining who to treat among people with chronic hepatitis B (CHB), first-line antiviral therapies for CHB, and strategies for preventing mother-to-child transmission of HBV using antiviral prophylaxis.
